name: Tactile Coding Systems
region: Global (Andes, West Africa, France, Polynesia, Mesopotamia)
summary: Non-visual encoding systems using knots, beads, notches, and raised characters to store and transmit information without dependence on sight or literacy.

claims.statement: Quipu knot systems, West African bead encoding, and Mesopotamian clay tokens represent independent inventions of tactile data storage
Braille (1824) succeeded where previous tactile scripts failed because it used a combinatorial cell structure rather than raised Roman letters
Tactile systems are inherently resilient: they function in darkness, require no electricity, and are accessible to visually impaired users

evidence.source: Schmandt-Besserat (1992) Before Writing: From Counting to Cuneiform, University of Texas Press
Urton (2003) Signs of the Inka Khipu, University of Texas Press
Braille (1829) Procédé pour Écrire les Paroles, la Musique et le Plain-Chant au Moyen de Points
Jiménez, Olea, Torres & Alonso (2009) Biography of Louis Braille and Invention of the Braille Alphabet, Survey of Ophthalmology 54(1)
WHO (2023) World Report on Vision — Braille literacy and accessibility metrics

notes: Promoted from candidate. Resolves a key cross-link: quipu → tactile_coding → low_bandwidth_data. Demonstrates that accessibility and resilience are design properties, not afterthoughts.
